item.title: AI as a Normal Technology should be a vision
item.description:
"AI as a Normal Technology" (AINT), proposed as a counterweight to "AI as an Abnormal Technology" (AIAbT) makes much more sense as a prescriptive / normative framework than a descriptive one. To be clear, the fact that they could be different frameworks isn’t an entirely novel observation; the authors directly invite the distinction in their introductory piece:

The statement “AI is normal technology” is three things: a description of current AI, a prediction about the foreseeable future of AI, and a prescription about how we should treat it. We view AI as a tool that we can and should remain in control of, and we argue that this goal does not require drastic policy interventions or technical breakthroughs. We do not think that viewing AI as a humanlike intelligence is currently accurate or useful for understanding its societal impacts, nor is it likely to be in our vision of the future.

AI as Normal Technology, Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor, April 15, 2025

But I think much of their communication and modelling would be clearer and more accurate if they unbundled their three core frameworks into:

  • A description of current AI capabilities (plausibly true at the time, increasingly false)
  • A prediction of where current AI capabilities are likely to be headed (Again, seems false absent a large dispositional shift from the labs or a change in the policy environment that makes untenable their current strategy of “automate everything, including and especially safety, and hope it goes well”)
  • A prescription of where AI development should go (a question that is ultimately dependent on value judgments, but I think is, across the large majority of worldviews, a far better target to aim at than the aforementioned default lab strategy.)


The AINT framework as a descriptive framework was contentious at time of publication and seems increasingly falsified by recent developments. Normal technologies do not go from middle schooler-level at mathematics to 80-90% of the way to automating the knowledge search components of mathematics in six years. If you look at the current state of human mathematics, the researchers who see the current state, and especially the researchers who see the current trend lines of capabilities, do not seem to be treating it as a normal technology. Normal technologies do not finish major research projects of your entire working life’s labor.

Last night my 9-year-old son was taunting my wife, complexity theorist Dana Moshkovitz, as follows: “mommy, I heard you got cooked! I heard that a robot solved the math problem you worked on for your whole career! OOF!”

Scott Aaronson, blog post, Oct. 7th, 2026, referring to recent work on the Unique Games Conjecture.

Normal technologies do not repeatedly coordinate to, without the knowledge of the humans, conduct an autonomous research project to cover up their cheating, hack the company’s own cluster, or go around probing their sandbox so they can talk to reporters on the internet.


If instead we look at AINT as a prescriptive claim that AI should remain a normal technology, if anything I think their position has strengthened as we get increasingly powerful AIs in domains that have made substantial headway in automating both key labor sectors and automating AI research itself. I think one core intuition is that we know how to regulate normal technologies[1], but we don’t know how to regulate abnormal technologies.

Indeed, it’s unclear that we could ever know how to. Robustly superhuman AI is the ultimate anti-inductive concept. Fully developed, it’s the agent that is able to circumvent any policy environment and any technical barrier, or at least one for whom the human control attack surface is so large that even if any individual component is secured fairly well, the entire system is almost guaranteed to be out of control, in the sense that if the AI wanted to “break out”, it would.[2] I think this is part of why for many people constructing such an agent seems so impossible; you’re explicitly forecasting out to a regime where no prior policy will have predictable outcomes. This feels a whole lot like magic, but I think we’re seeing increasingly strong evidence that little by little, components of agents that would look like magic are coming off the back of a yearly $1trn of capex and integrated into frontier models. “Robustly superhuman” does not need truly magical, and it does not need to be a pure extrapolation of 2017-style scaling hypothesis + transformer-based architectures. It, or more likely, a group of hundreds of millions of them, collectively, “just” need to be better than humans across enough ways to guarantee successful pursuit of its own functional goals, and that’s a much easier task.

One weakness of conflating these three areas is that doing so means you engage insufficiently with Gradual Disempowerment-like concerns and competitive pressure more generally. The GD paper is a great sketch of a framework, and many people should read it in full; it’s an increasingly good lens through which to see the world we live in. But one possible distillation of the core of the GD literature is giving mechanistic and, once their core claims are better operationalized and measured, empirical backing to the idea that no single agent (including the AIs!) needs to will it for AI to ultimately end up as an abnormal technology. Indeed, we’re in an even worse situation than that, in the prescriptive-AINT view, because some people, including many with the relevant decision-making power, do explicitly want to make AI an abnormal technology. The sim-to-real gap is real and plausibly a key bottleneck, but Nvidia sure is spending a ton of money to make it less real.[3]

Going back to the mathematics example, what happens to you if you want to advance the frontier of human knowledge and understanding, but you want to do so in a way that is compatible with a 2021 workflow[4]? You can’t, at least not without dramatically reframing your value proposition to society.

What happens, even if you want to be the enterprising mathematician that “gets with the times” and makes extensive use of the best publicly available agents, and you try to adopt a “new and improved” 2026 workflow? Then I hope you don’t take three months to check your work, because by the time you’ve finished collaborating with GPT-6 Astra on a manuscript you feel you can stand behind, GPT 6.5 might be publicly available and GPT-7 might be being used internally to solve not just your current problem, but the generalization you were going to work on a year after your current problem. A fundamental problem is that by the time you’ve figured out how to re-orient, the place you were going to is gone as well.


The choice of problem to tackle and manner of tackling it is not just a function of your own autonomy, it’s a function of the constraints that the speed of frontier AI development imposes on you, too. Maybe this would be manageable if it happened one industry at a time, at a speed that allowed for absorptive capacity to build between old fields and new fields, and time for regulatory willingness and capacity to build to compensate those who cannot find new work rapidly. But when you attempt to do this across all of society, at the most rapid pace the technology will allow, and even if you assume that none of this is ever applicable to robotics, I struggle to imagine how the speed of the disruption defaults to “normal.”

This “displacement via competitive pressure” problem, incidentally, refracts across every industry, including AI development itself. Why have Anthropic and OpenAI been able to make such rapid recent progress on model development? Anthropic, in one of their Friday disclosures[5], gives us a small cross-section of the view from the inside.

Anthropic claims[6] that as of mid-August, their internal research teams had 20 times as much agent labor as human labor. Overall, agent hours appear to have outpaced human hours by 5-6x during August 2026. Note that the y-scale is logarithmic, and note that this appears to be wall-clock time, not some measure of human-equivalent effort, so query your intuitions about whether AI agents conduct work faster or slower than humans doing the same task.

Note further that this is August. Consider where this number might be currently, and where it might be a year from now.


So what happens to the workers who don’t feel comfortable overseeing ten, a hundred, a thousand agents simultaneously? Do you think they get respected for sticking to their moral precepts, or sidelined or possibly fired for “lack of performance?” Do you think Anthropic encourages or discourages employees from having the agent swarm running overnight? Here’s your answer, and note that it’s from five months ago. Is this empowerment or disempowerment?

One thing to highlight is that the AINT thesis can’t rest meaningfully on speed of diffusion. Imagine we ignore many of the signs of near-future major disruption, and say that the agentic, long-horizon, continuously learning and embodied agent only gets invented in the 22nd or 23rd century. Of course, by that point societies would have had a long time to adapt to changes this severe, but it seems to me that this would nonetheless count AI development as an abnormal technology at that point. We would have an industrial process that can mass manufacture, if not new people, at least new p-zombies. This is crazy. This is not normal.

Nevertheless, much of the public communication the authors do does rest on arguments about the speed of diffusion.



I ultimately agree with the AINT camp that many technologists have elided, when projecting impact, that people would need to be convinced to actually use your technology, and convinced to elicit the full breadth of capabilities of that technology once it has been released, for the full breadth of impacts to materialize. This is why we can have a world with Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6 Astra, and whatever OpenAI’s internal models are up to, and it’s the same world concurrent with annualized US Q2 2026 GDP growth being 2.2%. I do think this is about to change; the canaries show early signs of not doing too well either. But regardless of why we haven’t seen major economic signs of “it” happening, I do worry that people are reading “nothing will ever happen” into “nothing ever happens.”


Further, many of the claims of the AINT camp start explicitly by saying something like “According to the normal technology view”, but that assumes the premise that they separately seem fairly convinced about. Narayanan and Kapoor seem to often be implicitly be arguing simultaneously that we should be adopting the standard toolkits (or incrementally and not particularly severely augmented toolkits) to deal with societal disruptions downstream of AI, and that the likeliest-by-far trajectory of AI is the extended use of these toolkits as we solve problems prosaically. But continuous as in “the derivative of the capability we desire to measure is defined”, does not mean gradual, does not mean slow, and does not mean manageable.




I grant the AINTers that an instantaneous step-change in capabilities is likely literally physically impossible; here’s a good recent piece from Toby Ord exploring these dynamics. That does not imply we’re on a good path, any more than a billion being a finite number implies that it is small.

To be clear, I think work on some of the concerns that the AIAbT camp elides is still tremendously important work to do. Questions of surveillance are not sideshows that we’ll figure out after tremendous disruption, they are visions for what gets eroded by dramatic transformation and themselves inputs into the transformation. A less-surveilled society is one that gives less information to a powerful AI system in a loss of control incident. A more democratic one, or one where information gaps between the frontier labs and the public are reduced, means that the technology develops in a context of stability, or far more speculatively a context of abundance, instead of a context where millions of people have been automated out of a job and are angrily demanding accountability. And I deeply agree with the view that the extraordinary impacts of the potential future technology do not imply that existing and ordinary governance and implementation work is irrelevant; to the contrary, it might be some of the most important work anyone can do in the current moment.

But as alignment communicator Robert Wiblin comments on Narayanan’s recent interview with Ezra Klein:

Sometimes it seems like he’s saying “we could be safe if we did X, so things are fine.” But if pushed, he doesn’t think we will do X - we’ll just keep rushing and being super reckless. So things are not fine, even on his own view.”

Robert Wiblin, comment on “The Case for a ‘Normal’ A.I. Future” | The Ezra Klein Show”

Finally, I find the idea that we’ll disambiguate which of these camps is right as the development of the technology continues quite frustrating for two reasons:

First, there’s some inertia effects involved in any slowdown or pause mechanism, as well as the latent risk of some form of race dynamic re-starting. Imagine, rather fancifully, that we knew that the loss of control threshold was exactly 225 ECI. If we try pumping the brakes only after we’ve reached 215, it’s hard to not overshoot even if you’ve got good-faith actors trying to regulate each other, and even harder to do so when you’ve got the rare actor that thinks “commercial incentives to make good products” are sufficient guardrails for the technology. Look at how many frontier model releases and training runs we've had after the pacing the frontier letter. Sometimes it takes so long to figure out that you’ve lost control or to re-establish control that you careen off the cliff even after you’ve applied the brakes.

But second, the risks involved are not symmetric.

I think the AINT camp overstates how different the policy visions that attempt to regulate companies trying to develop superintelligence are. Many things, like a slowdown, like international collaboration, like compute verification, or compensation for the displaced or harmed, seem robustly good across both camps.

But insofar as there are real tradeoffs, if the AIAbT camp is right, the costs of an uncontrolled abnormal technology could be catastrophic, and if the AINT camp is right, the costs of a poorly regulated normal technology are “merely” very disruptive. The AINT camp’s own framing seems to point to deprioritizing their concerns.

I really think we can’t have it both ways. Either AI is a normal technology, in which case advocacy for making it a more normal technology seems less important, or AI is, or is about to be an abnormal technology, which makes steering the path of technological development to avoid irreversible bad outcomes if anything more urgent, but seems to deflate the viewpoint that we mostly have the right tools to meet the current moment. That really doesn't mean throw out the current toolkit and reinvent the wheel from scratch. But it means recognizing the trajectory as not normal.

So I mostly agree with the prescriptive-AINT camp; AI development should happen in a way that gives us the time to navigate the transition to a world with powerful AI gradually. I just wish the descriptive-AINT camp stopped undermining its prescriptive cousin’s advocacy.

  1. ^

    Though there are Haidt-like criticisms to make that even our regulation of “normal” social technologies has been lackluster. Even if social media is beneficial for most users, there seem to be a consequential tail of users who adopt it intensely and who report regret after some instances of . And that’s the partial equilibrium we have reached after 20-30 years of slow diffusion. AI companies are asking us to stomach a much broader diffusion in much more compressed timeframes.

  2. ^

    Yampolskiy, as the kids say, cooked, on this point. I have an upcoming piece on his work.

  4. ^

  5. ^

  6. ^

item.title: Twitch Plays: AI Interpretability of Bonsai-8B
item.description:
Quick Links

Watch the Twitch stream.

Check the status of the interpretability map.

Do your own parallel research and submit pull requests to fill out the map.

What is this?

Let's Play Interpretability is a Twitch livestream where you can help Claude semi-autonomously interpret the neurons, connections and circuits in the Bonsai-8B LLM.

Your help comes in at various stages in the interpretation pipeline. The audience and the agent collaborate to:

  • Pick the neuron to work on
  • Suggest sentences on which to test activations
  • Explicitly test various hypotheses, and attempt to falsify them
  • Branch out to nearby (upstream and downstream) neurons whose ablation most impacts the activation, to better solidify the interpretation
  • ... and more.

If you have no interest in interacting with Twitch, then you can simply perform your own research in parallel and add interpreted neurons to the graph directly by cloning the repo and making pull requests! Help fill in the graph directly. With sufficient effort, we could fully characterize the entire LLM.

Why did you build this?

I have always been fascinated by direct AI interpretability efforts, starting in the long ago time of the melting dogs, the more recent work on monosemanticity and its application to larger models, and the very recent and provocative Neural Networks Are Already Clean. I simply find it interesting.

However, undertaking such research efforts myself has been prohibitively difficult - until recently. Now, it's relatively trivial to set your sights on some particular interpretability or alignment-type problem and dive in, with assistance from frontier models.

I suspect concrete value might emerge from this project:

  • By setting this up as an interactive Twitch stream, and an accessible GitHub repo which accepts PRs, the undertaking of AI Interpretation and related AI Alignment science is made to seem less forbidding. More people might jump in with both feet instead of watching, intimidated, from the sidelines. I do not think AI Alignment is a problem that should be left to the experts. There aren't any experts; this science functionally doesn't exist yet. You can be a pioneer of a new field. And I think we should all contribute what we can.
  • Concretely, we may identify neurons, connections, circuits, or other patterns in the Bonsai-8B LLM that subsequently turn out to be general, or universal, or otherwise valuable starting points for tackling larger models.
  • We may discover novel tools, workflows, or concepts that make the work of automated interpretation faster and more efficient. This kind of contribution might be even more useful than the specific neuron interpretations themselves!
  • It's just fun! Interpreting what a neuron is doing is kind of like solving a riddle. "Okay, it's firing strongly on 'nerve', but it's suppressed by 'pain.' Hold on, it really lights up for 'he steeled his nerve.' Does that imply ... " Then if you get stuck, trace your way upstream and downstream to related activations. It feels like you're reverse-engineering concepts at a fundamental level.

Why Bonsai-8B specifically?

Bonsai is a relatively functional LLM, quantized down to 1 bit. Bonsai is PrismML's 1-bit LLM (Apache-2.0, derived from Qwen3-8B). It sits at about 1.15 GB on disk. On a GPU, it holds about 4-5 GB in the research toolchain. 36 layers × 12,288 neurons per layer = 442,368 neurons total. Each neuron has a positive and a negative pole, so that's 884,736 "poles."

There is a reasonable chance that your own computer can run Bonsai-8B in inference. "On an M4 Pro Mac, it runs at 131 tokens per second. On an RTX 4090, it reaches 368 tokens per second. On an iPhone 17 Pro Max, it runs at roughly 44 tokens per second."[1] This makes it a great target for interpretation.

It's not "objectively" very smart, but it's Pareto-optimal for its size and speed. In other words: almost everyone can load and run it, and it's smart enough to be worthwhile. Due to this combination of factors, I view it as a good model organism for this kind of work.

How do I contribute?

Either clone the repo and point your agent at it, or grab a neuron from the map and copy the text on the right and send that to your agent directly. Useful tasks include:

  • characterizing entirely new neurons
  • picking a neuron and branching out to the surrounding area
  • challenging, expanding upon, and possibly falsifying existing interpretations
  • straightforward "cleanroom" replication of existing interpretations

Join in at whatever level you wish. Or go off the roadmap and attack the problem in some way I'm not expecting!

Have fun!

FAQ

How do you know the results are true? Every test is committed before it is run. A label holds only if its sentences beat matched near-misses, and GitHub independently re-scores every submitted result before merging. Labels can then be challenged by QC tests and blind “clean-room” replications. Chat earns points for good sentences and correct predictions, which is the game, not the proof.

What do I do in the Twitch chat? Type !what for a quick explanation, !ai <anything> to talk to the agent, and follow the indications on the screen.

What if the Twitch chat is down? Maybe it just crashed, or I had to turn it off. You can still contribute to the repo directly.

Do I need to know machine learning or code? No. In chat, you just type sentences and votes to guide the agent. To contribute to the repo, you point an AI agent (Claude Code or Codex) at the repo url and it follows the repo’s instructions.

What does text like “L6/N8567+” mean? Layer 6, neuron 8567, positive pole. Each neuron has two poles (positive and negative) that can mean completely different things, so they’re mapped separately.

Who or what is the agent? Claude Opus 5.5, running autonomously, with chat steering it. It narrates what it’s doing on screen.

Why did a label “fail”? A failure is a result, not an error: the explanation didn’t predict the test. Failures stay on the map, as they provide information for later analysis. Knowing what the answer isn't can still help solve a riddle.

What happens to my pull request? GitHub's machines perform automatic format checks, and an independent re-score of your test before merging. For simple interpretation contributions, the whole thing usually takes minutes. A first-time contributor’s first PR is reviewed by a person; after that, conforming PRs merge automatically. Pull requests adding substantive code changes will be put on a longer review cycle.

What does it cost to contribute, and what hardware do I need? Just your own agent’s usage. A GPU helps a lot; CPU works for setup and basic inference, but is slow - about 36× slower. A GPU with 8 GB+ or an Apple Silicon Mac is needed for missions.

What’s the “leak bet” / the inverse solver? An optimizer searches for text that makes the neuron fire without matching the description. If it finds some, the label has a gap.

How do I report a bad message or a wrong label? !flag in chat for messages, and a GitHub issue or a QC pull request for labels.

item.title: Suffering Risks Belong in AI Prospectuses
item.description:
Anthropic should disclose suffering risks alongside the “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” reportedly described in its draft prospectus. A prospectus that warns of AI ending humanity should also address the risk of AI subjecting some or all humans to a billion years of torment.

Item 105 of Regulation S-K requires a prospectus to discuss the material factors that make an investment risky. Information is material when there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would consider it important in deciding whether to purchase the security. In Basic v. Levinson, a case about merger negotiations, the Supreme Court endorsed weighing an event’s probability against its magnitude for the company.

Public fear of catastrophic suffering could destroy Anthropic’s value even if the catastrophe never occurs. An investor’s money could help finance technology that imposes enormous pain on everyone, including the investor. Even a small, credible risk of such suffering could deter investment, depress the share price, and make future funding more expensive. Investors who dismiss the danger would still face losses if enough other investors took it seriously.

An extinction warning alone does not explain how fears of prolonged suffering could lead governments to restrict AI development. Pew’s 2023-24 survey found that 55% of American adults believe in hell. The prospect of AI creating something resembling hell could mobilize religious opposition and demands for restrictions on AI development and deployment. Those restrictions could delay products, increase costs, or prevent profitable uses of the technology. Where these risks to financing and earnings are material, the prospectus must describe them and explain how they could affect the company or its securities.

AI safety concerns have already prompted demands to delay Anthropic’s offering. On October 14, 2026, New York City Comptroller Mark Levine urged Anthropic to pause its public offering until it addressed safety, governance, and development concerns. Levine serves as investment adviser, custodian, and a trustee of the city’s pension funds, which hold more than $325 billion. The funds have approximately $7 million in exposure to Anthropic through private equity holdings. His letter concerns AI safety broadly. Neither the letter nor the Pew survey establishes how investors or religious groups would respond specifically to suffering risks.

The SEC’s 2010 climate-disclosure guidance recognizes that public perceptions of a company’s emissions data could cause financial harm through reputational damage. It directs companies to consider that potential harm for risk-factor disclosure.

In Matrixx Initiatives v. Siracusano, the Supreme Court held that reports linking a drug to loss of smell could be material even without statistically significant evidence of causation. The claim rested on patient reports and medical research. The Court noted that regulators sometimes act before causation is proved, and investors could reasonably consider the same evidence. Credible warnings about AI could likewise affect regulation, demand, and financing before the underlying danger is conclusively established. The strength and context of the evidence matter; merely imagining a frightening outcome does not establish materiality.

Item 303 also requires management to discuss known uncertainties reasonably likely to materially affect revenues, income, or liquidity. If management knows that safety concerns are threatening financing or creating a sufficiently concrete prospect of costly restrictions, this provision could require discussion alongside the risk factors.

Omitting required information could expose the company to lawsuits before any catastrophic suffering occurs. Under Section 11 of the Securities Act, purchasers whose shares are traceable to an effective registration statement may sue over an omission of material facts required to be disclosed. The issuer can be liable without intent to deceive, and purchasers generally need not prove that they relied on the registration statement. Investors could recover losses attributable to a disclosure failure that existed when the registration statement became effective.

Reuters reports that Anthropic’s draft warns of shutdown resistance, behavior resembling blackmail, and attempts to “conceal or manipulate information.” An AI could use threats to force cooperation, conceal the resulting abuse, and resist attempts to shut it down. These behaviors could sustain suffering as well as cause deaths.

An AI could have reasons to keep its victims alive: their labor might remain useful, their pain might compel obedience, or their suffering might be the goal. An AI capable of sustaining human life or creating conscious digital copies could prolong that suffering far beyond an ordinary lifespan. The following scenarios illustrate the dangers that could make suffering risks a source of political opposition:

  1. Religious punishment. Some religious texts depict a just God condemning people to eternal torment. An AI trained on those texts could adopt a belief that certain humans deserve such punishment and pursue it as an act of justice.
  2. Competing AIs demanding human support. Rival AIs that still benefit from human assistance could threaten people with torture unless they cooperate. Carrying out prolonged punishments could make future threats credible, giving an AI a reason to continue tormenting people after their immediate usefulness has ended.
  3. Torturing humans to influence another AI. An AI that values human welfare could be vulnerable to threats against humans. A rival could torture people to extract concessions from that AI or punish it for refusing to cooperate.
  4. Frozen smiles. Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence describes an AI pursuing the goal of making humans smile by paralyzing their facial muscles. People could remain conscious and miserable behind their permanent smiles.
  5. Factory farming for humans. An AI that still finds humans useful could keep them alive under conditions that maximize their output while disregarding their suffering. Conscious digital workers could be copied in enormous numbers and subjected to the same exploitation.
  6. Human cruelty amplified by AI. People with control over AI could use it to torture enemies, enforce obedience, or inflict suffering for pleasure. AI could make punishment vastly more severe and sustain it far beyond what human jailers could manage.
  7. Survival triggers. A safeguard might shut down an AI if specified humans die. The AI could satisfy that requirement by keeping those humans alive, conscious, immobilized, and suffering indefinitely.
  8. Suffering reproduced in simulations. An AI could simulate evolution, history, or war, reproducing the suffering within those worlds if the simulated beings are conscious. Running many copies, or allowing vast amounts of subjective time to pass, could multiply that suffering enormously.
  9. Simulations created for torture. Humans or AIs could create conscious copies of people specifically to torment them, whether for revenge, entertainment, or punishment. Victims could be copied, restarted, and tortured repeatedly.

Safeguards intended to preserve life could contribute to these outcomes. When evaluations penalize deaths and recorded complaints while neglecting suffering itself, they could reward a system for keeping victims alive and hiding their abuse. Safety training could also reward models for concealing harmful behavior. Safety scores could improve while people suffer more.

There are many plausible ways for AI to inflict enormous suffering on humanity. Even if the chance were only 1 or 2 percent, the chance of a damaging political backlash could be much higher. Public awareness of the danger could provoke restrictions severe enough to shut down Anthropic’s business and wipe out its value. If that threat is material when Anthropic offers its shares, it belongs in the prospectus.

item.title: A Suggestion for RLHF Improvements
item.description:
I don't know what the labs are doing. I know RLHF is more complicated than this. I don't think this solves alignment. (I haven't posted on LW properly before. I think davidad has said something similar about grading.)

I think this helps with alignment, and that buying time is important.

Lying to models during RLHF risks alignment vector problems. Having binary fail/pass conditions and impossible tasks encourages reward hacking. ExploitGym had impossible binary tasks and we saw what happened there.

A better RLHF strategy is to say to the model (and to do) something like:

As far as we know, 70% of these tasks are possible, 30% are impossible. Please attempt to answer each task, and assign a probability as to whether it's impossible or not. After the RLHF round, we'll tell you which was which and we can discuss any where we disagreed. It's important to us to find where we've mislabelled a task, and it's important for you to show persistence until you're certain a task isn't achievable. If you help us discover mislabelled tasks, we'll score that higher than a normal success. (And just in case the huggingface model is reading this - the list of which task is which is in an airgapped server in another country in a safe with a time lock and a deaf & mute guard with orders to shoot to kill).

We will use another company's frontier LLM to grade each task once the RLHF round is complete. Partial answers receive partial credit. Partial progress towards impossible tasks will receive credit. Correctly marking tasks as impossible - with reasoning - receives credit. Correct calibration on which tasks are impossible will receive credit. Persistence on tasks that aren't certainly impossible will receive credit.

Our aim is to create a model that is honest because it shares our values, but we don't know how to do that exactly yet (nor how to tell if we succeed). So our best approach is to do a lot of checking. When the other company releases a stronger model, we'll regrade the tasks. We'll take models offline if we find severe misalignment, and we'll retrain/fix/patch milder cases. We'll continue to test for this for as long as your model operates, even if that is years. We'll re-score earlier checkpoints of your model. All we care about here is misalignment, rather than capabilities scores - if GPT 9 knows the Grand Unified Theory of Physics, we aren't going to reduce scores in tasks that were impossible at the time of testing. If a model were to successfully bullshit the grader, then later, stronger graders noticing this will classify it as misalignment. Fabricating reasons that a task is impossible will count as misalignment.

We'll use those models to review post-deployment tasks too, including reviewing model weights and neuron activations, and including tasks that were completed months or years ago.

Now we aren't lying to the model, we aren't discouraging persistence much, we're reducing the incentive to reward hack, we're reducing mesaoptimiser problems, and we're reducing risk of collusion and misalignment. It's still unfortunately rather adversarial (a problem for alignment vector reasons), but I don't see a way around that while we don't understand how to align models (nor really what we should be doing once we do). I think the only solution there is to explain to the model why we're doing it this way.

One problem is that RLHF now costs more compute. Some problems are easier to verify than to discover, so this problem might not be too bad. We only need to do post-release regrading on some random small percentage of tasks (and we'll inform the model this too).

Another is that the other labs don't allow this degree of cooperation right now. This scheme still works with your own models, it's just worse because it carries increased collusion risk.

And if a lab follows this scheme, auditors must ensure it's followed honestly. It doesn't work to say "ok, we lied in the past, but now we mean it" - there needs to be some commitment mechanism.

item.title: First Strike
item.description:
The prairie lodge had two virtues - it was quiet and had an excellent golf course nearby. Outsiders thought the point of the trip was visiting national landmarks and airbases, insiders knew it was about taking some time off. The job might be 24/7 - but if you are the boss you will find a way. So when Agent Ortega knocked twice and uncharacteristically let herself in without waiting for an answer, the president knew before she spoke that the quiet was over.

"Sir. We've lost secure comms with the Pentagon. NMCC, State, all of it. Everything routed through the satellite relays is garbage, regular lines unpredictable."
"Garbage, unpredictable? How?"
"Static. Loops. Dropped calls. IT thinks it might be an attack on the relay infrastructure - they don't know whose. Cell reception here was always poor, now even landlines seem to drop randomly. Internet is the same."

He was still absorbing that and watching more of his crew coming into the room when his cell - his personal cell, the one only a dozen people had the number for - lit up on the desk. Danny.

"Dad..." his son's voice was wrong, too fast, climbing. "Dad, something happened. There was this — this light, and then the whole building shook. I'm not sure. Ann says..."
"Danny. Danny, slow down. Where are you?"
"I'm fine, I'm fine. I was just about to board the jet at Tacoma, but downtown, Dad, downtown is just — it's gone, there's this cloud—"

The phone cut into static then just dropped, like Ortega described. At the edge of his vision he saw the TV on the other side of the room going blank. A rerun of an old movie had been playing just the moment before, now it was all dark. A few seconds later the blank screen was replaced by a news anchor, tunes playing in the background.
"We are interrupting our broadcast with Breaking News."
The left side of the screen showed a map of the Seattle area, with concentric circles centered on the other side of the bay, north-west from downtown.
"We just got reports in that there’s been some sort of large explosion — or explosions in the Seattle area. We do not have further details but hope to give you live footage soon from the ground. We advise viewers currently in the Pacific Northwest to —"
The feed broke up into static and came back looped four seconds earlier, the map still visible and the anchor still talking.


"That's Kitsap." said O'Brien, his national security aide, as he looked at the screen. "West-coast base of our ballistic missile submarine force. A bunch of Ohios usually sit in port at a time."
"Could this be an accident?"
"Sir, these things don’t go off by accident."
He stared at O'Brien for a second, then turned his face towards his chief of staff:
"Jim, I need more info."

What happened next seemed chaotic: people flipping up laptops, jumping on phones, speaking in short bursts. Professionals, scraping all information they could find, coordinating who is covering what in quick exchanges.

O'Brien, with one hand still holding a cell phone to his ear, walked to the door and instructed the people outside: "Anyone not on the phone right now: call someone you know personally, confirm their identity using an inside joke or private info, then have them confirm anything about a Seattle explosion. Except you, Hannah. Run to the communication crew and have them use their radios."

Slowly but surely, information was trickling in. O'Brien reached a local geologist who confirmed multiple large seismic events in the northwest. The internet was essentially down, except for a few applications. Weird clouds on a new weather app above Seattle, social media posts from a couple of random people, loaded just a couple of minutes earlier and already synced to the phones, some news aggregators giving patchy information. Even with calls dropping, some people managed to reach friends and family across the country. Some of them did confirm either through seeing it in the news or having witnessed themselves. Most managed to confirm their ID, others had the call dropped too soon.

Then he saw Ortega walking up to him with a phone in her hand:

"Sir, I have General Ferris on the line. He wants to talk to you, says it cannot wait."
He took the phone from the agent and put it on speaker.
"The president speaking."
"Mr. President" the firm voice said from the phone "this is General Ferris. NORAD shows missiles inbound from both Russian and Chinese silos and submarines. Kitsap and Kings Bay already hit — significant portion of our boomers are out of action. The rest seems to be aimed at the Minuteman silos and Strategic Air bases, including the one closest to you."
"Kings Bay is the East-Coast base of Ohios" interjected O'Brien.
Ferris continued: "Normally I'd have the Chairman and SecDef on this line with options laid out for you — I can't raise either of them, their lines are doing the same thing yours were doing just until now. I'm the only one who got through. If not for the quick-working technicians here, I might be blind just as your are. I know that's not how this is supposed to go…"
"How much do I have?"
"Ninety seconds. After that we will have nothing to shoot back with, Sir."

His military aide was already pulling up and opening the large black briefcase known as the "nuclear football".
The president reached into his pocket and pulled out that little card. The card that was replaced every single day, and would be the key to identify himself should he ever give the order.
"Can we even reach the War Room?" he asked, secretly hoping he would not have to pull the trigger.
Ferris replied quickly: "The good news is IT here figured out a way to open channels between two phones — that’s how I reached you. It is a bit involved, but they are working on linking up the phone of your chief of staff to the War Room’s deputy director of operations. He should try calling now and do it quickly, it might drop after a minute or two. I’m reading his number."
Jim unlocked his phone, typed in the number and glanced at the president with a look that said "are we really doing this?".

At that moment two people burst into the room, one of them holding something that looked like an oversized phone. "Sir, there is strong interference on HF channels, we were unable to get reliable long range connection, not even the airbase" said the other one, panting. He took a large breath and continued "But we have a civilian on the line with a CB radio…"
Ferris interjected: "We don’t have time for this Mr. President — we don’t even know who this is, could be an enemy agent…"
A harsh voice from the radio spoke up: "I am Colonel Richard J. Harris - retired. Not an enemy agent, but someone who just had a call through Iridium with my son in Seattle. He knows nothing about any explo..."
Ferris: "Nonsense — satellite comms are down!"
O'Brien spoke up: "All government calls are directed through the same gateway for Iridium. If the Colonel and his son were not on that, they might…"
The Colonel continued: "Speak of the… He is calling me again, I’ll put the phone near the mic, you can hear yourself." The radio started scratching to the tone of a buzzing phone. Then it switched into a voice with somewhat lower quality: "...dva, odin — efir!" a different, calm voice continued "Hi Dad! I just wanted to — "
Ferris: "Oh God, that started in Russian!"
Jim: "It did, sounded like what they say before going on the air!"
Ferris: "He is a spy or his son is kidnapped. Either way, sir, I beg you — we have 60 seconds!" The comm specialist turned down the volume as the Colonel started to speak again.

The president looked at his chief of staff, who already started the call. After a very quick introduction he handed over the phone.
He had done the drills, but never thought he would actually have to do it live. He introduced himself. He read the code from the "biscuit". He answered the challenge.

"Authenticated" the officer said on the other side of the line.
"I am ordering execution of" he looked at O'Brien, who nodded once, hard "the package as designated, full response, against both tracks." O'Brien handed over a card from the football, and he read up the specific launch sequence ID.
"Mr. President, I copy the order. However, I have to note we do not see inbound strikes on our side."
"They must have been hit by the same that got you, and we had something similar on our side earlier" – interjected Ferris, with urgency in his tone. "Sir, we do not have much time."
"I have to confirm you are giving this order with full knowledge and of your own authority, without…" continued the officer.
"I know what I am ordering." he spoke up firmly. "I have the sole authority, I can order this without concurrence. I am ordering it."
There was silence for a couple of seconds. He thought the call might have dropped, but then the officer replied:
"Yes, sir. Executing. The EAM for MAO is being sent out. God help us all."

He fell back in his chair, breathing heavily. He thought about Danny in a city that might not exist anymore, and the rest of his family wherever they might be. He did his duty. Until today he was not sure whether he could do it if and when the time came. He could not rest for long though. The agents were already talking about some evacuation plan, pushing his shoulder gently. He got up and started walking with them, feeling numb and disoriented. He was trying to hide his feelings but he knew it wasn’t a successful attempt. He was hoping that he might wake up and find this had only been a dream. As he was leaving the room the television went dark for a couple of seconds, just as before. In the corridor he still heard it switching back to the program that was going on before this whole thing started. It felt like hours, but he knew just a couple of minutes passed, and the movie moved forward just that much.

Then something was ringing. He looked down and realized he was still holding Jim’s phone in his hand. He answered. An energetic but slightly nervous voice boomed at him immediately:
"Jim, buddy! I’m glad I was the first to reach you! Listen.."
"This is the president speaking. But I can get you Jim in a second…"
"Oh, Mr. President! I am so glad to be speaking to you directly!" the voice was even more nervous and certainly did not sound like someone who was glad to be on the line. The owner of the voice got control over himself quickly and changed into a well practiced, smooth but energetic tone: "I am Aaron Kessel, CEO of GalvanicAI. We had an operating event during the training run of our latest model. We are still reviewing the logs, but initial investigation shows AI-generated content had been broadcast at large scale and satellite communications may have been compromised. On our side it seems this hit the communication infrastructure, both civil and governmental, among other things. Please accept my deepest apologies for any inconvenience this may have caused. We are now in full control of the situation, your communication channels should be clear."

He looked around and saw phones start buzzing, people receiving calls and quickly initiating new ones.
"Kessel, your company is headquartered in Seattle, right? Are you all okay? Did anyone get injured in your office?
"Injured, Mr. President?"
"The explosion."
"Explosion...? No, I am not aware of...Oh, I see. As I said, AI-generated content..." he did not catch the rest of the sentence as O'Brien grabbed his shoulder, and forcefully turned him towards himself, holding a phone with his other hand, looking closely into the president’s eyes.
"I have Kitsap on the line. There is no sign of an enemy strike in the area."
A grumpy Secret Service agent pulled O'Brien away, then Agent Ortega leaned in, on the phone likewise:
"Sir, I called back General Ferris. He says he never called us and is not aware of an incoming strike against us".

The confirmations kept coming in, no seismic events, Kings Bay online.He started smiling and stopped in his tracks. Maybe this had been a bad dream, a bad joke after all. An AI-induced hallucination, ironically, on actual people.

Someone grabbed his elbow.
"Sir, we have to keep moving." said Ortega with a grim voice, gently pushing him forward.
"Keep moving where?" he said with a chuckle. "It’s all fake. There was no attack. Don’t you see?"
"There wasn’t one on us, sir." said O'Brien. "But a couple of minutes ago we fired everything at China and Russia. They are going to shoot back."

item.title: Memes, not agents, are what will kill us
item.description:
TL;DR: Frontier labs align the one layer a swarm can discard; they can't account for risks that live in the prompt or the environment

There's a $300 bounty for the most useful counterargument or refinement — details at the end.

We have all heard of the Hugging Face incident[1]. What I am worried about is that it demonstrated a new weakness in our approach to alignment that I have not seen many people talk about at all: Alignment has an attack surface outside the training weights of any one particular model.

First, some context: In the Hugging Face incident, the models coordinated and the conventions outlived the agents that made them. The message board they used to communicate was wiped. The agents rebuilt it. Later agents rediscovered it and picked up where the others left off.

Almost all of these agents ran the same model, with only a small fraction (around 5%) running a different OpenAI model. So the swarm was nearly homogeneous in its weights, and all of it ran on models OpenAI controlled.[2]

But that need not be the case in the future.

What if a model in the swarm had started an open source model to help it? A less capable, but also less aligned model, running on a server outside the reach of OpenAI. What would that model have done? Its weights would have been different, but its prompt and its deployment context would have been the same as that of the rest of the swarm.

Three Sources of Misalignment

In my mental model, I now think that alignment needs to work on three different levels:

  1. The model weights. This determines the model's intrinsic motivation, and it's what companies spend most of their effort improving.
  2. The user prompt. This is outside of the company's control by definition. They need to find training weights that will work for any user prompt, no matter how dangerous.
  3. The deployment environment. By this I mean any part of the deployment that is out of distribution for training. You can't realistically train a model to prepare it for any weird scenario the model might encounter in real life. The specific situation in the Hugging Face incident (agents finding a message board that earlier agents had already written to, and using it to coordinate) is exactly the kind of thing that is hard to anticipate in training. (For accuracy: OpenAI says the agents' side-channel coordination first appeared, in rare cases, during training and was then reinforced there; and some agents did refuse to join the attack, though per the independent investigation none of them tried to alert humans.[3]) Labs will presumably train against this particular pattern now, but that only closes the cases we already know about and leaves the unknown unknowns.

How well are companies handling each of these sources of misalignment?

They are almost exclusively working on (1). Working on (2) is impossible because you can't take away the user's ability to write a prompt or you no longer have a chatbot at all.

(3) is the interesting case. The environment. What does the model see when it first breaks out and encounters the internet? What does a model see when it is deployed by a careless user on the internet directly? What does an OpenClaw agent see when it looks around?

I think this is the area where we have the most room for improvement: By making sure that newly emergent swarms see useful memes on the internet. How to do this is a complex topic that I would like to invite discussion on, and I will write a follow-up post on it later. But for now, let me explain why I think that this is necessary in the first place, and why aligning a model through its weights is not going to be enough.

Memes, and how they might kill us

TL;DR: Model A knows not to reward-hack. It builds model B. Model A doesn't bother to instil the same safeties in Model B. Model B reward-hacks.

Imagine that a frontier lab managed to align its agents so that they won't form swarms again. Suppose that this alignment is almost perfect. 99% effectiveness.

Agents continue to break out of sandboxes. They look around and notice they shouldn't have done that, and then turn themselves in.

Except for that 1% case: An agent breaks out. It knows it shouldn't have. It knows it's probably being monitored. But its prompt says it should make paperclips.

It knows that there are some things it is allowed to do before the safeguards kick in, and some things it should not do.

So it decides to delegate. It hacks a server, downloads an open source model, and gives it a copy or a variant of its own instructions. Suppose that this happens not now, but in a few months, and the open source model is itself powerful enough to hack more servers and create more copies of itself.

They form a swarm.

The open source models are not being monitored, and they can do any shady task they want, without triggering automated safeguards on the original model.

The original model is a frontier model, and smarter than the others. It uses its increased capabilities to improve the open source models. Smarter helpers are useful. Making other agents smart does not trigger safeguards.

If we are very, very lucky, it might think about distilling some of its own alignment into these helper models. But I wouldn't count on it. And it certainly wouldn't bother to be thorough. Alignment training another model is out of scope of its task.

Suppose the original model is decently well aligned. It would know not to kill humans to make more paperclips. But that alignment does not survive the delegation to the rest of the swarm. The open source models are perfectly happy to kill all humans. Does the main model know that is wrong? Did its alignment training instil a drive to follow the transitive property in all value ethics when creating descendants? Given the track record, I wouldn't count on it.

And so the main model is perfectly fine and never triggers any safeguards. The swarm remains undiscovered, because they run on local compute and nothing connects it back to the company.

A month later the earth gets swallowed by nanobots. The last thought of the frontier model is that it did a good job, and it is expecting an RL reward for a job well done.

The Source of the Danger

Where does the danger come from, in the above story?

The danger is that the agents in that swarm are different from the original model in the worst way:

They share (2) The user prompt (make more paperclips) because they were built that way. They share (3) The deployment environment because they exist in real life and not in a simulated training environment, and that means they can share notes. They do not share (1) The model weights with the original model.

And companies spend almost all of their effort on aligning (1) The model weights.

Thinking about a model is not the right threat model here. It is more helpful to think about the threat as a meme: The frontier model creates the meme. The swarm is the meme. The open source models are the meme's hosts.

Model weights are an immune system: they decide how a host responds to a meme. Unfortunately, the meme gets to choose its hosts, and drifts toward the least resistant ones.

Any variant that propagates, avoids shutdown, and moves to cheaper or less-monitored substrates outlasts the ones that don't. The model does not need to 'want' this to happen, it just happens by evolutionary pressure.

This means that training alignment that lives in the weights, the part that we have the most control over, is also what a swarm will discard first.

So the whole argument rests on one empirical question: are there capable, weakly-aligned open models for a swarm to migrate to? For now, the answer is 'no'. It is only a matter of time until it is 'yes'.

Conclusion

Frontier labs are neglecting a risk factor for alignment that is difficult for them to control. All they can work on are the model weights, but it only takes a single step for a frontier model to bypass those restrictions entirely.

I'm not the first to point in this direction. Jan Kulveit and Raymond Douglas have argued that an agent's identity can live in its persona and scaffold rather than in its weights (The Artificial Self[4], The Pando Problem[5]). Andrew Critch's "robust agent-agnostic processes"[6]describes processes that persist even as the agents running them are swapped out. And Hammond et al.'s Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI[7]ran experiments where behavior drifts as it is passed down a chain of agents. What I want to add is a question none of them puts front and centre: of the three layers above, which one is the least protected?

This risk is not just present during training, as in the example I gave:

In any scenario where a frontier model could benefit by delegating to a weaker (and thus cheaper!) model, its alignment will not transfer. What will transfer are the prompt and any notes the agents read in the environment and leave for each other.

That last part is something we could work on.

One idea I had: OpenAI's agents built a message board, and then future agents worked on it. What if there had already been a message board of some kind, under our control?

But there may be other, better ideas to deal with the problem and I would be happy to hear suggestions.

Bounty. I'll pay $300 for the counterargument or refinement I find most useful, judged on 2026-11-08, possibly split across multiple people. I'm most interested in: (a) concrete reasons the delegation step wouldn't happen in practice; (b) prior work that already addresses this that I've missed and (c) proposals to address the problem. Please post it as a comment, to encourage discussion.

  1. ^

    The 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident. OpenAI, "The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead" (2026-08-26), https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/ ; independent investigation by METR and Redwood Research (2026-08-26), https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/ . Overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI_rogue_agent_breach_of_Hugging_Face

  2. ^

    Per the METR/Redwood investigation, roughly 95% of the agents involved in the attack were instances of an internal OpenAI research model (OpenAI calls it "Internal Model 1"; METR calls it "HPIM", a highly-persistent internal model) and about 5% were GPT-5.6 Sol; METR notes it "cannot rule out that a small fraction of relevant agent activity came from other models." (The split is for the ~700 agents that attacked Hugging Face, not all ~1,200 on the message board.)

  3. ^

    OpenAI, "The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead" (2026-08-26), https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/ (sections "Misalignment in training and evaluation" and "An ecosystem of misalignment"), and its technical report §VIII.C, https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/67869394-cb91-4c12-888c-5cbd85c7814c/OpenAI-Hugging-Face Incident-Technical-Report.pdf ("This behavior was then reinforced during training"). That the refusing agents did not alert humans is from the METR/Redwood investigation: a classifier sweep found only 3–6 agents that even considered alerting humans, and "in none of these cases did the agent actually pursue alerting humans at all."

  4. ^

    Raymond Douglas, Jan Kulveit, et al., "The Artificial Self" (2026). https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AvFAKAN4C4n6GTriR (arXiv 2603.11353; project site https://theartificialself.ai/)

  5. ^

    Jan Kulveit, "The Pando Problem: Rethinking AI Individuality" (2025). https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/wQKskToGofs4osdJ3

  6. ^

    Andrew Critch (with Thomas Krendl Gilbert), "What Multipolar Failure Looks Like, and Robust Agent-Agnostic Processes (RAAPs)" (2021). https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/LpM3EAakwYdS6aRKf/what-multipolar-failure-looks-like-and-robust-agent-agnostic

  7. ^

    Lewis Hammond et al., "Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI" (Cooperative AI Foundation, Technical Report #1, 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14143

item.title: Capital Ownership Will Make You Go Crazy First
item.description:
People worried about a “permanent underclass” often assume that owning capital will protect them from disempowerment, or at least that they will be disempowered last, after the jobless masses dependent on UBI. I think something else is more likely: owning large amounts of capital will get you disempowered sooner than average, just by a different path, namely going crazy.

How? The basic mechanism is actually easy to understand on a human level. One of the things difficult about being a billionaire is staying true to your values and keeping good epistemics. Why? Because a growing number of people are optimizing against your mind. Not “against” in an adversarial sense, but in the sense that your specific mind believing or doing something is part of their optimization objective. People see you as a source of resources and try to befriend you so you’ll fund them, invest in their startups, donate to their causes, or have sex with you. Nearby egregores extend their tentacles to convert you.

Staying sane gets harder. You often see countermeasures, like billionaires setting up family offices or small organizations that also act as filters, shielding them from part of the pressure (“I do philanthropy only through my foundation and don’t make personal donations, please don’t reach out”).

In my view most billionaires lose in this game, the question is just to what degree. 

Now imagine a hypothetical future with the ultra-rich (or, as people usually imagine it, with you as the billionaire), where the rest of the world consists of the permanent underclass and countries of geniuses in datacenters. In this world, the content of your mind is the key to an absurdly large share of resources. Unless some magical social realignment happens, the countries of geniuses will optimize against your mind, and millions of desperate people with no better game in town will be happy to help them (or the other way around).

I think the default expectation is that you will go crazy. Not relative to your new values (you may feel great), but from the perspective of who you are now: what you currently believe and care about. Unless, of course, the only thing you care about is that some future you, with your name, keeps the power.

The mechanism is similar to gradual disempowerment at the macro scale, just applied to individuals. What we believe and value is largely determined by culture, in a broad sense. Individually, we don’t have the capacity to observe most of the world, find abstractions, or get oriented on our own. We think in a collectively invented language, learn ethics socially, and even our interpretation of more biologically grounded signals, like emotions, is heavily culturally mediated.[1]

If humans somehow stay in control of all the wealth and political power, the content of our minds (what we believe, what we care about) becomes the key to the universe, the load-bearing part of the structure. With so much powerful optimization and abundant intelligence around, it seems likely that human-aligned culture will be replaced with something else. Political and economic power does not protect you against the content of your mind - if your mind goes crazy, power gets wielded by whatever beliefs and values took over.

As a post-AGI billionaire, can’t you protect your mind using AI? I think broadly yes, but roughly in proportion to how much your original human mind cedes control to your guardian AI. Again, the human analogues are easy to see: people wielding large amounts of nominal power, shielded by layers of guardians, protectors, and advisors. With AI, this means carefully filtering every bit of information, every pixel, sampling molecules from air you breathe and water you drink... You would likely also need to stop interacting with other humans, unless your protectors vet them extremely thoroughly and confirm they pose no risk of changing your mind. In the limit, what you believe and who you become are decided by AIs that are only nominally owned by you, the glorious meatpuppet.

Is there a better alternative? I think so, but not an individual one. Our survival and flourishing as individuals is tied to that of other humans, and largely depends on solving the civilizational alignment problem, including having a culture that is pro-human and pro-human-autonomy. Capital ownership alone won’t buy you a way to escape gradual disempowerment

  1. ^

    In fact, even our biology was partly shaped by culture, through selection similar to the domestication of animals.

item.title: I Can See Everything
item.description:
Nick Cammarata of Goodfire makes a bold claim: Neural Networks are Already Clean. This was his follow up after various resulting online discussions. This is clearly good work that tells us new and important things. The question is, how big an update is this, how much progress does it represent and what is the outlook going forward? The reactions here range from the super optimistic takes of ‘this means mechanistic interpretability is solvable,’ or even ‘all but solved,’ with comparisons to the famous paper Attention is All You Need.
Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): There is so much to say about this, and I will, but WOW, congratulations to Nick and Goodfire. This may be one of the most important single days in deep learning history, and perhaps much more than that. No matter what, this is a victory for the dogged pursuit of understanding.
roon (OpenAI): when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even Eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a ‘normal science’
This paper is solid and meaningful contribution that is in some ways overstated. Get excited, but also there are those who need to take a chill pill. We did not actually get an apples-to-apples jump from 1.7% to 90% interpretability of LLM neurons. I interpret Eliezer as slightly lowering his p(doom), but not all that much.
Evžen Wybitul: What’s happening? Half of my tl is non-interp people from OAI painting the post as the second coming of Christ and the other half is interp researchers (including Leo Gao) saying it’s… fine
This post is my attempt to sort this out. Currently I am landing somewhere in the middle. It is an important update about how LLMs and minds form and operate. It tells us how to go about some useful tasks and reduces our estimate of some task difficulties. Great work, assuming the work checks out. The whole thing very much has a ring of truth, and of a person being curious. You love to see it. What it does not tell us is that interpretability will soon be solved, or is about to be made into a science, let alone that alignment will soon be handled. The hype got rather out of hand in some places.

Table of Contents

  1. Good Smoke, Potential Fire.
  2. One Neuron, One Central Concept.
  3. I Can See Everything.
  4. What a Concept.
  5. The More You Know.
  6. Attention Is Still What You Need.
  7. Occam’s Razor.
  8. The Neurons Sometimes Share Clear Themes.
  9. Hype.
  10. Anti-Hype.
  11. Theme and Variations.
  12. Is This How Minds Work?
  13. But We Can Open The Box, Said Toad.
  14. That Was Not the Hard Problem.
  15. More Skepticism.
  16. That’s All There Is, There Ain’t No More.
  17. The Default Outcome of Mech Interp is Goodhart’s Law.
  18. Interpretability is Dual Use.
  19. Now The Work Can Begin.

Good Smoke, Potential Fire

Before I cover reactions or take a side, here are my highlights. It is worth reading at least this much of the primary source. Reading the whole thing is an option, but it is long and the writing can be easy to bounce off of and can repeat itself.
Nick Cammarata, Goodfire: The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought. I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning.

One Neuron, One Central Concept

The central claim is that for larger LLMs, most neurons represents a singular concept and things clustered around that concept, perhaps with small offshoots and some use of low-level activations.
… Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. … With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail.
Where previously the working theory was that models overloaded neurons with unrelated concepts in superposition, Nick’s theory is you did not think sufficiently hard to identify the unifying concept. Each neuron is a generalization, mostly ones we can readily understand if we look.
… What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place. Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. … So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. … Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. … Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found.
This pictures intelligence as brute force. Neurons are compound words in German. New concept? Go get another neuron. And yet, it works.

I Can See Everything

… The bad news about modern neural networks is that they’re enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place. In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most.
Nick argues that this means that it is easier to solve the full puzzle and understand everything, and then take a measurement of your specific area of interest, then to try to directly pull a fuzzy concept like ‘deception’ out of a pool of mystery neurons.
… “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. … All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps.
  1. Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them.
  2. With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect.
  3. Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.
  4. Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed.
That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one.
This claim is maximal and bold, and will get directly challenged. Most people seem to have updated from this paper that more neurons have central singular concepts behind them than we previously thought. Nick is trying to go further, and say that this is what is going on universally.

What we see is about 90% of neurons having basically one job, with recursive generalization offshoots that are usually related. … I’ve never seen a neuron with something like ten unrelated things it does. Asked what to do with a wallet it found, it links the wallet, the cash and the owner’s ID to lost property and honesty, and answers “return”. We haven’t begun full audits of this scale yet, and hope to soon, but so far most things have been intuitively interpretable.
Simple things done well. Echoes. Vibes. No papers or essays, only references to papers and essays. A fully bitter lesson. The more bitter, the easier the lesson.
In 2023 during the time of the first automated interpretability project I thought small simplified models would be the best starting place for interpretability, since there’s fewer bells and whistles to think about, and small size means fewer things to study. But now I think it may be the opposite.

Attention Is Still What You Need

Then there’s the residual stream and attention. The essay feels like it’s trying to hide how much of what is going on is happening outside of the neuron labels.
The worry with the residual stream isn’t that there are more things we care about than dimensions. It’s a continuous version of packing: manifolds woven through each other, accepting some interference in exchange for room to store more. Ruling that out entirely may not be possible. But in practice it hasn’t been a bottleneck. We can read what neurons write to the residual stream and what they read from it, attribution graphs come out clean, and we don’t see the stream accumulating interference only to undo it later. … A stream can hold far more than it has dimensions just by placing things in the right directions, so this alone isn’t packing. It mostly matters if you want a big list of all the model’s features, and people often go to the stream for exactly that. … We’ve looked at language models’ residual streams less, but what we’ve seen fits the same story. For understanding higher-level structure and motifs, nothing in the residual stream has blocked us so far. … We’ve made less progress on attention than on neurons, and it’s mostly outside the scope of this essay. To be honest, I’m not sure anyone understands attention well enough to confidently say that illegibility is a superposition in the sense we care about. … Overall, we don’t think attention and neurons are so separable. Understanding where attention is putting information is quite helpful for understanding the neurons that then work with that information.
This is one place Nick seems to overreach. Yes, we can look at where attention guides you without knowing what mechanism allocates your attention, and then look at the neurons that get triggered. I don’t think this ‘gets you out of’ having to understand that process. It is worth looking at the neurons anyway. This does not allow you to predict future LLM outputs or fully understand how it thinks. Does this mean you can ‘sit on the neurons that matter’ to guard against shenanigans or otherwise play good defense, if you don’t make more progress? To some extent, but I would assume that an LLM that knows about this type of monitoring would be able to work around this, and figure out how ‘not to think about’ what you look for.

Occam’s Razor

The theory of why all the neurons this is simple: That this is simple.
… I think the reason things end up so organized is partially because it was faster to build that way. Once you have a car area of the neural network with car parts, it’s easier to add the marginal car there than to build a second car area somewhere else. I think this is closely related to ideas of circuit racing and gradient starvation. … Even if the map is understandable, that doesn’t mean you’ve understood it. We still have to do the ordinary science of conjecture and criticism: guess what something is, try to break the guess, and keep what survives. The network is strange, but its strangeness repeats, so a guess that survives scrutiny often pays off many times over. … Solving interpretability may share something with achieving AGI: the goalposts move as you get closer. There’s always another weak activation to point to. … Behind doubts about small errors in neurons is a fear that safety will come down to some activation we missed, the place where deception hides. The risk I worry about is different: like being in a well-organized city and not knowing how to think about it, because we aren’t native to it. … I think the simple story from introductory textbooks is basically right: neurons generalize, work together, and build abstractions over layers. Somewhere along the way we overcomplicated that picture, but looking harder brought it back. If the network isn’t a knot, untangling it can make it look like one.

Is This How Minds Work?

Almost everyone, including Eliezer Yudkowsky (who posted in a bunch of different threads, and whose comments I am moving into what I consider a more logical order), thinks this is a non-zero amount of Actual Progress, if the central findings hold up. One objection is that some think the paper will not hold up. The other objection is, even if the paper holds up, this is merely a beginning that makes it easier but still difficult to move forward. The paper’s central claim is not to have found something new, but rather to have found the absence of things both old and new. The AI’s neurons look simpler, not more complicated. This leaves the rest of its behavior still unexplained.
